descriptionChirho: The act or state of sin itself — moral failure, transgression, or offense against God; the dominant sense of חַטָּאת covering the majority of occurrences across all grammatical inflections (singular/plural, all pronominal suffixes, construct chains, prepositional prefixes), rendered consistently as English 'sin', Spanish 'pecado', Hindi पाप, Arabic خَطِيئَة/خَطَايَا, Korean 죄/죄들, Swahili 'dhambi'.

The sacrificial offering prescribed to atone for sin — a technical cultic term prominent in Leviticus, Numbers, and Ezekiel; distinguished by English 'sin-offering', Spanish 'ofrenda por el pecado', Hindi पापबलि, Arabic ذَبِيحَة الخَطِيئَة, Korean 속죄제, Swahili 'sadaka ya dhambi', and invariably occurring in ritual/sacrificial contexts describing the preparation, slaughter, or presentation of the offering.

The penalty or consequence visited upon the sinner as a result of חַטָּאת — distinguished by English 'punishment', Spanish 'castigo', Swahili 'adhabu' (punishment), in contrast to the act of sin itself; parallels the punishment sense of עָוֹן (H5771) and appears in prophetic judgment contexts where the focus shifts from the transgression to its divine retribution.

A rare specialized sense referring to the means of ritual purification — the 'water of purification' (מֵי חַטָּאת) in Numbers 19:9,17 involving the ashes of the red heifer; distinguished by Spanish 'purificación', Swahili 'utakaso' (purification/cleansing), and Korean 속죄, where the focus is on cleansing from corpse-contamination rather than a blood sacrifice or the act of sinning.

An anomalous or metonymic usage where חַטָּאת is rendered as shame or disgrace rather than sin proper — marked by English 'peoples' (likely a translation anomaly), Korean 수치 (suchi = shame/disgrace), and Swahili 'aibu' (shame), suggesting either a contextual extension where sin is equated with its resulting public shame, or a possible textual confusion with a different lexeme.
